Show HN: Type-C – variants, options, generics and pattern matching for C
show_hn.story_text: I love C, but often using it for parsing, tree walking or complex error handling leads to spaghetti code. Of course there is Swift, Ocaml or Rust for situations like that, but then you are either forced to convert the entire codebase, or add a runtime library or go through the pain of bridging C to the new language.  Sometimes there are no compilers for the target architecture too when you are working on embedded stuff. This is where Type-C comes in.  It works as a preprocessor like TypeScript and calls the original C driver behind the scenes.  Your code stays normal C for the most part, so you can predict how the code will be laid out. Photorealistic image inspired by Milo Manara's tenebrist figure studies, realized as a 1990s analog photograph at a Milanese covered-market food stall in the pre-dawn dark, February 1994.
SUBJECT: A 22-year-old brunette with dark hair loosely braided over one shoulder, working alone before opening. She lifts a heavy batter bucket onto the counter with both hands, catching her own reflection in the stainless steel and pausing mid-lift to regard the camera with a quiet, private smile — unguarded, faintly sleepy, entirely herself because no customers are present to perform for. Attire is modest and period-specific: an oversized thermal waffle-knit sweater in oatmeal with sleeves pulled over her palms, high-waisted charcoal corduroy trousers, thick wool socks inside clogs, a bib apron already tied and slightly dusted with flour, a hand-knitted scarf still looped at her throat from the walk over. Her breath is faintly visible in the cold air. Thermos mug steaming on the counter edge.
SETTING & ERA DETAILS: An iron-and-glass covered market with every other shutter still down — rolled corrugated steel, padlocks, stacked wooden crates, hanging bunches of dried herbs, enamel signage, a mechanical cash register under a cloth cover, a wall calendar showing February 1994, a rotary phone on a hook, a single delivery trolley abandoned in the aisle. Wet cobblestones outside gleam under distant streetlamps. No phones, no card terminals, no other staff.
LIGHTING (CHIAROSCURO): One bare work lamp clamped to the stall frame provides the only key — a hard, warm pool that illuminates her face, forearms and the batter bucket while the entire market hall beyond falls into impenetrable black. Light spills across wet tile in a long tapering wedge. Steam from the thermos crosses the beam and glows. Absolute value range; perhaps eighty percent of the frame is true darkness, which makes the small island of illumination feel theatrical and intimate. Form defined almost entirely by where shadow begins.
CAMERA & EQUIPMENT: Shot on a 1990s Canon EOS-1N using Kodak T-Max 400 film pushed one stop to 800. 85mm f/1.8 EF lens at f/2.2 for gentle compression and shallow separation. Tripod-mounted, deliberate composition, medium shot from waist to crown, camera at chest height angled slightly downward toward the counter. Fine structured grain with strong acutance on her eyes and the metal surface.
POST-PROCESSING & COLOR GRADING: Near-monochrome grade with a restrained warm sepia cast concentrated in the lamp pool and a cool graphite tone creeping into the surrounding void. Contrast printed steep through the midtones, blacks crushed deliberately so the market's depth reads as pure absence rather than detail. Soft highlight roll-off preserves texture in the steam and flour dust. Optical vignetting deepens all four corners; a faint emulsion base-curl mark along one edge. Should read like a photographer's personal frame made during a long assignment, kept back from the published set precisely because it is too quiet.
